alalal-e77569-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 3: whether the definitions of faith given by Dionysius and Hugh of Saint Victor are well assigned.

alalal-e77569-d1e120.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) definition: faith is the virtue by which things not seen are believed.

alalal-e77569-d1e132.summary: Notes that other similar definitions are found alongside this one, of which two will be considered.

alalal-e77569-d1e142.summary: Gives Dionysius' definition from the Divine Names: faith is the unique foundation of believers, placing them in truth and truth in them, by which believers have a simple knowledge of truth in credible truth.

alalal-e77569-d1e160.summary: Gives Hugh of Saint Victor's definition: faith is certainty of absent things, set below knowledge of truth and above opinion.

alalal-e77569-d1e174.summary: Notes that other definitions appear later in the second part.

alalal-e77569-d1e181.summary: First objection to Dionysius: faith is not the unique foundation, since humility also founds; and if humility founds the humble not the believers, every virtue would be a foundation in its own way.

alalal-e77569-d1e199.summary: Second objection: faith places us in a mirror and enigma rather than in truth.

alalal-e77569-d1e210.summary: Third objection: faith is below knowledge of truth, so it does not place us in truth.

alalal-e77569-d1e222.summary: Fourth objection: 'placing truth in them' cannot mean faith places truth in us through faith, since then faith would be agent, medium and instrument of the same act.

alalal-e77569-d1e246.summary: Fifth objection: truth is in vision, not faith; we walk by faith and not by sight, and are pilgrims from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6-7), so faith makes us wander from truth rather than placing it in us.

alalal-e77569-d1e270.summary: Sixth objection: how can believers have simple knowledge of truth in believed truth when there are so many articles in both creeds?

alalal-e77569-d1e290.summary: Turns to objections against Hugh's definition, faith as certainty of absent things.

alalal-e77569-d1e299.summary: First objection: 'absent' means either absent in place, but such things may be present to reason, or absent to reason, but what is not present to reason cannot be certain to it.

alalal-e77569-d1e319.summary: Second objection: placing faith below knowledge makes it less certain than moral virtue, which the Philosopher says is more certain than any art and so than any science.

alalal-e77569-d1e342.summary: Third objection: opinion is a habit of imperfect certainty fearing the contrary, so it is not comparable with faith.

alalal-e77569-d1e362.summary: Fourth objection: is faith above or below demonstrative science? It seems above, since martyrs die rather than deny faith while philosophers did not die for what they knew; yet faith rests on authority, which is the weakest topic and produces only opinion, so faith seems even below opinion.

alalal-e77569-d1e406.summary: Solution: Augustine's definition in the text is disputed by Lombard himself, so its treatment is deferred.

alalal-e77569-d1e417.summary: On Dionysius: his definition describes faith by its proper effects in the believer. As first by nature in the spiritual building, it founds and places us in the truth of the article and of hoped-for beatitude; as a kind of cognition, it places the truth of the article in us by most certain consent; and since its truth is not complex like a principle of syllogism, believers have simple knowledge, a simple light that makes them know the truth of the articles somehow. So faith does three things: founds us in truth, founds truth in us, and gives simple knowledge of truth through a light like first truth.
claims: Faith founds us in truth, places truth in us by certain consent, and gives simple knowledge through a light resembling first truth.

alalal-e77569-d1e472.summary: Reply to the first objection: humility does not found as laid in the foundation but as digging deep trenches by emptying itself, in which the foundations are laid.
claims: Humility prepares the ground for faith, which is the foundation.

alalal-e77569-d1e485.summary: Reply to the second: faith places truth in us by holding it through the assent of cognition, but not through sight; truth is in mirror and enigma as object and end, not as in its own light.

alalal-e77569-d1e504.summary: Reply to the third: 'knowledge of truth' there means vision through species, clear and open truth, but here truth is meant as veiled in mirror and enigma.

alalal-e77569-d1e517.summary: Reply to the fourth: faith places truth in us through the consent and cognition it produces, not through faith itself; that cognition is of mirror and enigma.

alalal-e77569-d1e533.summary: Reply to the fifth: truth is in both faith and vision, but differently; it is ascribed to vision because there it is unmixed with likenesses.

alalal-e77569-d1e544.summary: Reply to the sixth: though the articles are many, one thing underlies them all, first truth; so faith is a simple light, a likeness of that truth, not composed of many like the light of intellectual science.
claims: Faith is one simple light because first truth underlies all the articles.

alalal-e77569-d1e562.summary: On Hugh: 'absent' means absent to reason, in two ways: wholly unknown, neither as object nor proved, which the objection assumes; or present as object but without a proving and convincing reason. Faith is certainty of the absent in the second sense, as the Gloss on Galatians 5:6 calls it certainty of the invisible: the proving reason is lacking, yet consent is strongest.
claims: Faith is certain assent to objects present to reason but lacking a proving reason.

alalal-e77569-d1e608.summary: Reply on moral virtue: faith is more certain than any art or moral virtue; 'knowledge of truth' in Hugh means contemplation through species in the Word, which surpasses all certainty, not the knowledge of art. The objection equivocates on 'knowledge of truth'.
claims: Faith is more certain than any art or moral virtue; only beatific vision exceeds it.

alalal-e77569-d1e629.summary: Reply on opinion: faith surpasses opinion. Augustine names three aids of the intellect in divine matters: opinion, liable to error, as whether those rising with the Lord were later reduced to ashes; faith, owed to authority backed by revelation of the Holy Spirit; and understanding, owed to clear reason. Faith is the mean in this sense only.
claims: Faith rests on authority grounded in the Holy Spirit's revelation, placing it above opinion.

alalal-e77569-d1e664.summary: Reply on authority: faith is led by the hand by the authority of the fathers who bought it, but does not consent because of that; it consents because of truth itself, without reason. In this it is above opinion, which consents for a reason while fearing the contrary.
claims: Authority leads to faith, but faith consents because of truth itself, not because of the authority.

alalal-e77569.summary: Article 3 tests two definitions of faith alongside Augustine's, which is deferred. Dionysius calls faith the unique foundation of believers, placing them in truth and truth in them and giving simple knowledge of truth. Hugh calls it certainty of absent things, below knowledge and above opinion. Albert reads Dionysius as defining faith by its effects: as first in the spiritual building it founds us in truth, through certain consent it places truth in us, and as a simple light like first truth it gives simple knowledge. It is one because first truth underlies all the articles. Humility digs the trench for this foundation, and truth is in faith veiled in mirror and enigma, unmixed only in vision. On Hugh, 'absent' means present to reason as object but without proving reason. Faith is more certain than any art or moral virtue, below only beatific vision. It surpasses opinion because it consents for the sake of first truth itself, the authority of the Fathers only leading it by the hand.
claims: Faith founds believers in truth, places truth in them by certain consent, and gives a simple light of knowledge.
Faith is one because first truth underlies all its articles.
Faith is certainty about objects present to reason without a proving reason, more certain than any art or moral virtue but below vision.
Faith is led by authority but consents because of first truth itself, which places it above opinion.
